Types of Skeletal Muscle
Skeletal muscles receive innervation from the peripheral nervous system.
Skeletal muscles affect volitional control of the axial and appendicular skeletons.
Unipennate, bipennate, and multipennate muscles
Unipennate: insert on one side of a tendon with fibers arranged to insert in a diagonal
direction onto the tendon (eg, lumbricals)
Bipennate: insert on two sides of a tendon, facing in opposite diagonal directions, with a
central tendon, which provides a larger cross section and greater strength than an
unipennate muscle but allows for smaller changes in length (eg, rectus femoris)
Multipennate: multiple rows of diagonal fibers and a central tendon that branches into two
or more tendons (eg, deltoid)

Types of Skeletal Muscle
Skeletal muscles affect the volitional control of the axial and appendicular skeleton,
receiving innervation from the peripheral nervous system. Skeletal muscles can be
categorized based on their insertion into the tendons and the distribution of myofibers.
Muscles with parallel fibers are most common and experience a substantial change in
length with relatively little force; however, their relatively small cross-sectional area
results in a relatively small production of force. Fibers of a unipennate muscle insert on
only one side of a tendon, with their fibers arranged to insert in a diagonal direction onto
the tendon. This creates a relatively large cross section and greater strength but less
change in length. Examples of unipennate muscle include the lumbricals and the
extensor digitorum. Bipennate muscle fibers consolidate on two sides of the inserting
tendon, facing in opposite diagonal directions, with a central tendon. This results in a
larger relative cross section and greater strength compared with an unipennate muscle
but smaller changes in length. The rectus femoris is an example of a bipennate muscle.
Multipennate muscles have multiple rows of diagonal fibers and a central tendon that
branches into two or more tendons. An example of a multipennate muscle is the deltoid
muscle, which has three sections: anterior, posterior, and middle.

Muscle Structure
Skeletal muscle fibers and connective tissue (Figure 1)
Skeletal muscle fibers are highly specialized multinucleated cells characterized by a collection
of contractile filaments called myofilaments.
Filaments are organized in a defined hierarchy, with the basic functional unit of muscle
contraction being the sarcomere.
The largest functional unit is the myofibril, a string of sarcomeres arranged in series.
Adjacent myofibrils are connected by a set of specialized proteins called intermediate
filaments that allow for mechanical coupling between myofibrils.
Epimysium: connective tissue covering the entire muscle
Perimysium: connective tissue surrounding collections or bundle of muscle fibers, or
fascicles
Endomysium: connective tissue surrounding individual fibers

Muscle Structure
Each skeletal muscle unit is enclosed in fascia to allow for smooth motion past
surrounding tissues. Each muscle is comprised of bundles of muscle fibers called
fascicles, which are enclosed by epimysium, a connective tissue covering the entire
muscle just deep to the overlying fascia. Each fascicle is composed of hundreds of
muscle fibers and is surrounded by another layer of connective tissue called the
perimysium. Endomysium is the connective tissue surrounding individual fibers. Each
individual muscle fiber (myofiber) is subsequently enveloped by perimysium. Each

myofiber is a highly specialized, multinuclear cell that is a thin, tubular structure, often
many centimeters long, and usually spans the entire length of the muscle. Myofibers are
characterized by a collection of contractile filaments called myofilaments. Myofilaments
are structured in a defined hierarchy, with the basic functional unit of muscle
contraction being the sarcomere. The largest functional unit is the myofibril, which is a
string of sarcomeres arranged in series. Adjacent myofibrils are connected by a set of
specialized proteins called intermediate filaments. They allow for mechanical coupling
between myofibrils.
Cell Membrane Systems
A specially designed membrane system exists within the cell that aids in activating the
contractile properties of the muscle cell. The system consists of two main components: the
transverse tubular system and the sarcoplasmic reticulum (Figure 2).
The transverse tubular system begins as invaginations of the cell plasma membrane
(sarcolemma) and extends into the cell, perpendicular to its long axis. It relays the activation
signal from the motor neuron to the myofibrils.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a system of membrane-bound sacs that collect, release, and
reuptake calcium stores to regulate the muscle contractile process.
Calcium channels and pumps are contained within the sarcoplasmic reticulum and are
regulated by a complex enzymatic system.
The portion of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that abuts the transverse tubules (T-tubules) is
called the junctional sarcoplasmic reticulum.
The T-tubules and the two adjacent sacs of the junctional reticulum together are called a
triad.

forms invaginations into the cell, perpendicular to the long axis, surrounding the

muscle fiber an efficient contractile apparatus. Smaller longitudinal tubules extend from

on and off. The permeating design of the sarcolemma and the sarcoplasmic reticulum
increases the cross-sectional area, permits quick transmission of action potentials to the
contractile elements, and provides a reservoir of calcium ions close to the contraction.
Sarcomere Composition
Sarcomeres are composed of two major types of contractile filaments.
Myosin (thick filaments) and actin (thin filaments)
Active interdigitation of these filaments produces muscle contraction via a shortening
translation of the filaments.
The arrangement of these filaments also creates the characteristic alternating bands of
light and dark seen via microscopy.
Tropomyosin is a protein that twists around two actin strands in double-helix configuration
(Figure 3).
In the resting state, tropomyosin blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin.
Troponin is a complex of three separate proteins that is closely associated with tropomyosin.
If troponin binds calcium, a conformational change in the troponin complex ensues.
This results in a conformational change in tropomyosin, exposing the myosin-binding sites
on actin.
A resultant contractile protein interaction occurs, and muscle contraction is initiated.

Sarcomere Composition
Myofibrils are divided into contractile units called sarcomeres. Sarcomeres are
composed of two major types of contractile filaments: myosin (thick filaments) and actin
(thin filaments). These two sets of filaments interdigitate and interact to produce a
shortening translation of the filaments, resulting in muscle contraction. The sarcomeres
are highly ordered and are arranged in parallel along the long axis of the cell, which
produces contractions as a cumulative effect. The thick filaments are primarily
composed of myosin, a large protein consisting of a long, insoluble helical portion and
two globular portions called cross-bridges. They also contain C protein, M protein,
myosin, titin, and creatine kinase. The thin filaments are composed primarily of the
protein actin, along with troponin and tropomyosin. Tropomyosin is situated between
two actin strands in double-helix configuration. Troponin is a complex of three separate
proteins that is closely associated with tropomyosin. The arrangement of these filaments
also creates the characteristic pattern of alternating bands of light and dark sections
observed under microscopy.

H-band contains only myosin. The I-band is composed of only thin actin filaments, which
are joined to an interconnecting set of structural proteins (the Z-line) and extend into the

of individual thick and thin filaments remains the same. The thick and thin filaments
bypass one another, resulting in increased overlap. The A-band length stays the same,
the I-band reduces in length, and the H-zone reduces in length.
Muscle Contraction
The shortening interactions between the thick and thin filaments produce muscle contraction.
The globular domain of the myosin molecule hydrolyzes adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to
adenosine diphosphate (ADP), causing a conformational change in the myosin molecule that
pushes the filaments past each other.
Myosin then releases actin to return to original conformation.

Muscle Contraction
The longitudinal shortening interactions between the thick and thin filaments
cumulatively produce muscle contraction. The myosin molecules in the thick filaments
form cross-bridges with the actin molecules of the thin filaments. In the resting state,
tropomyosin blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin. If troponin binds calcium, a
conformational change in the troponin complex ensues, resulting in a conformational
change in tropomyosin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin. The globular domain
of the myosin molecule hydrolyzes ATP to ADP, causing a conformational change in the
myosin molecule that pushes the filaments past each other. The myosin molecule
quickly releases the actin molecule and returns to its original conformation. This ATP-
dependent cycle repeats in rapid succession to cause the thick and thin filaments to pull
toward each other. Because of the relative polarities of the thick and thin filaments,
active cross-bridging results in a sliding of the thick and thin filament complexes toward
each other and a shortening or resistance to stretching of the sarcomere.

Cross-bridge cycling is modulated by intracellular calcium via the regulatory protein’s
troponin and tropomyosin. Tropomyosin is a molecule on the thin filament that prevents
myosin-actin interaction. Troponin is a calcium-dependent regulatory protein with three
domains: the troponin-C subunit binds calcium, troponin-T binds tropomyosin, and
troponin-I is inhibitory to the actin-myosin interaction. If troponin-C binds calcium, the
molecule changes conformation, relieving the troponin-I and tropomyosin inhibition of
myosin-actin cross-bridging. Therefore, if intracellular calcium levels are high, cross-
bridge cycling is active, and the myofibrils contract.

Every muscle fiber is contacted by a single nerve terminal at a site called the motor end plate

The number of muscle fibers within a motor unit varies widely.

Nerve-Muscle Interaction
A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron and all the myofibrils it contacts. Each
myofibril is stimulated by one nerve axon; however, one axon can branch and
stimulate multiple myofibrils. If the motor unit is activated, all the myofibrils of that
unit contract. The number of myofibrils in each motor unit may vary widely and range
from approximately 10 to thousands. In general, muscles that require fine motor
control have relatively few fibers per motor unit. Chemical transmission of the
electrical impulse passing down the cell membrane of the axon occurs at the motor
end plate, or the NMJ. This structure controls the initiation of muscle contraction and
is composed of the presynaptic axon, the synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic muscle
cell.
During the conversion of neuronal depolarization to muscular contraction, an action
potential from the motor neuron reaches the axon terminal, and calcium ions are
allowed to flow into the neural cell. This increase in intracellular calcium causes

Pharmacologic and Physiologic Alteration of Neuromuscular
Transmission
Pharmacologic and physiologic alterations may substantially impair or enhance
neuromuscular transmission. Two common drugs that act on the NMJ and disrupt
neuromuscular transmission include nondepolarizing and polarizing drugs.
Nondepolarizing drugs (eg, pancuronium, vecuronium, and curare) competitively bind to
ACh receptors, blocking neuromuscular transmission and muscle contraction. Polarizing
drugs (eg, succinylcholine) bind to the ACh receptor, causing temporary depolarization
followed by failure of the impulse transmission. Enzymatic ACh inhibitors increase the
duration of neuromuscular transmission. Enzymatic ACh inhibitors are divided into two
groups: reversible and irreversible. Reversible enzymatic ACh inhibitors (eg, neostigmine,
edrophonium) prevent the breakdown of ACh and allow prolonged interaction with the
ACh receptor. Irreversible enzymatic ACh inhibitors (eg, nerve gases, certain insecticides)
similarly prevent the breakdown of ACh and result in sustained muscle contraction.
Myasthenia gravis is a physiologic disorder resulting in a shortage of ACh receptors and
is characterized by severe muscle weakness.
Muscle Function and Physiology
Muscle Function
Nerve activation of muscle contraction (Figure 6)
A muscle twitch is the muscle tension response to a single nerve stimulus. If a second nerve
stimulus arrives after the muscle tension has returned to baseline resting tension, no
increase in muscle tension development occurs.
Absolute refractory period: the period during which no stimulus will produce a muscle
contraction
Relative refractory period: the period during which the stimulus required for muscle
activation is greater than the typical threshold stimulus level
Paired twitch—If a successive nerve stimulus arrives before the resting tension reaches
baseline, the tension rises above the level of a single twitch.

Muscle Function
A single action potential results in a quick contraction followed by relaxation. The length
of the contraction ranges from approximately 7.5 ms (for fast twitch myofibers) to 100
ms (for slow twitch myofibers). A muscle twitch is the muscle tension response to a
single nerve stimulus. If a second nerve stimulus arrives after the muscle tension has
returned to baseline resting tension, no increase in muscle tension development occurs.
The absolute refractory period is the period during which no stimulus will produce a
muscle contraction. The relative refractory period is the period during which the
stimulus required for muscle activation is greater than the typical threshold stimulus
level. A paired twitch occurs if a successive nerve stimulus arrives before the resting
tension reaches baseline, resulting in a tension that rises above the level of a single
twitch. This phenomenon is called summation (wave summation or temporal
summation). As the frequency of gross muscle stimulation increases, higher peak
tensions develop. A plateau of maximal tension eventually is reached, at which no
relaxation of muscle tension between successive stimuli occurs (tetany). Dissimilar from
nerve tissue, muscle tissue has no refractory period for the contractile mechanism; a
rapid sequence of depolarizations results in a continuous, tetanic contraction.
Skeletal muscle can develop varying levels of muscle force, although each individual
motor unit contracts in an all-or-none fashion. This graded response is controlled by
different mechanisms. In spatial summation, different motor units have different
thresholds of stimulation; therefore, more motor units are activated with increased

Types of Muscle Contraction
Isotonic: muscle shortens against a constant load; muscle tension remains constant
Isokinetic: muscle contracts at a constant velocity
Isometric: muscle length remains static as tension is generated
Concentric: muscle contraction results in decreased muscle length; this occurs if the resisting
load is less than the muscle force generated.
Eccentric: muscular contraction accommodates an increase in muscle length; this occurs if the
resisting load is greater than the muscle force generated.
Isotonic and isokinetic contractions can demonstrate concentric action or eccentric action;
however, isometric contractions do not fit the definition of concentric or eccentric action.

Types of Muscle Contraction
Muscle contraction types include isotonic, isokinetic, isometric, concentric, and eccentric.
Isotonic contraction shortens against a constant load, whereas muscle tension remains
constant. Isokinetic contraction shortens the muscle at a constant velocity. Isometric
contraction occurs if length remains static as tension is generated. Concentric
contraction results in decreased muscle length if the resisting load is less than the
muscle force generated. Eccentric contraction results in increased muscle length and
occurs if the resisting load is greater than the muscle force generated. Isotonic and
isokinetic contractions can demonstrate concentric action or eccentric action; however,
isometric contractions do not fit the definition of concentric or eccentric action.

Length-Tension Relationship
The length of the sarcomere at the time of contraction affects the amount of force produced,
depending on myosin/actin overlap (Figure 7).
During resting length, this overlap is at its greatest and results in increased cross-bridging and
greater subsequent force.
The force of contraction decreases exponentially as a muscle fiber is shortened or lengthened,
and the overlap is concurrently decreased.
Figure 7 Graph shows the relationship between tension and sarcomere length. The greatest
tension is attained at the normal muscle fiber length, at which the overlap between actin and
myosin is greatest. (Reproduced from Huard JU, Utsunomiya H, Ravuri SK, Philippon MJ: Form and
function of skeletal muscle, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations of Clinical
Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 231-239.)

based on muscle length. The length of the sarcomere at the time of contraction affects
the amount of force produced, depending on the amount of overlap between actin and
myosin molecules. During resting length, this overlap is at its greatest and results in
increased cross-bridging and greater subsequent force. The force of contraction

Force-Velocity Relationship
Under experimental conditions, a load is applied to a contracting muscle and length is
isometric until no change in length is observed (isometric length). As higher external load is
applied, eccentric contraction occurs: the muscle begins to lengthen, and tension increases
rapidly. If load is decreased from the isometrically contracting muscle, concentric contraction
will occur: the muscle force will rapidly decrease, and the muscle will shorten in length.
Progressively decreased loads result in increased contraction (Figure 8).
Concentric contraction—The force generated by the muscle is always less than the maximum
force of the muscle. As seen in a force-velocity curve, the force drops off rapidly as velocity
increases. For example, if the muscle velocity increases to only 17% of maximum, the muscle
force has decreased to 50% of maximum.
Eccentric contraction—The absolute tension quickly becomes high relative to the maximum
isometric tension. Eccentric contraction generates the highest tension and the greatest risk
for musculotendinous injury. The absolute tension is relatively independent of the velocity.

Force-Velocity Relationship
The force-velocity relationship is a noteworthy contributor to skeletal muscle mechanics.
The velocity of muscle contraction is related to the load placed on the muscle: the larger
the load, the lower the velocity at which the muscle can contract. Conversely, muscle
velocity increases with a light load. This relationship applies only to the initial concentric

Skeletal muscle arises from mesodermal somite tissue. Early muscle progenitor cells are
called myoblasts, and the fusiform cells that eventually fuse into multinucleated cells are
called myotubes. Many contractile elements appear in the cell at the approximate time

stretch increase in length. Initially, the myofibrils and sarcomeres of a stretched muscle

tension curve shifts to produce peak tension at a greater length and to produce less
passive force if stretched. Conversely, greater passive force is generated by the same
stretch if a muscle is shortened for a prolonged period of time. Clinically, the mutability
of muscle length has been applied advantageously in surgical limb-lengthening and
muscle transfer procedures.

Aging and Senescence
Age-related skeletal muscle decline and atrophy are characterized by increases in
connective tissue, intermuscular adipose tissue infiltration, and disturbed muscle
metabolism. The myotubes and muscle fiber contractile capacity (type I and type II)
become impaired with progressive lipid deposition.14 The precise clinical role of
intermuscular adipose tissue infiltration is not completely understood; however,
evidence suggests that muscle decline is associated with adiposity, age, and localized
inflammation.15 Inflammation and lipid redistribution also have synergistic effects on
skeletal muscle and physical dysfunction and frailty. A shift in metabolic processes
promotes an imbalanced environment between perpetrating adipose tissue and muscle
and also contributes to muscle atrophy and dysfunction. Localized metabolic alterations
of skeletal muscle can promote senescence processes via apoptotic resistance, elevated
senescence associated-secretory phenotype (eg, metalloproteinases, proinflammatory
interleukins), and reactive oxygen species.14,16 For example, satellite cells play a pivotal
role in muscle regeneration in coordination with immune cells and nascent muscle cells.
On activation, which is driven by immune-cell signals, satellite cells proliferate and fuse
to regenerate muscle fibers and then return to a quiescent state for downstream
regeneration.17 Aging disrupts this process, leading to the induction of cellular
senescence, which likely results in inflammation and loss of proliferative ability of muscle
progenitor cells during muscle regeneration. With aging, progenitor cells display a
senescent phenotype typified by expression of the cell-cycle inhibitor p16.

Pharmacologic Modalities
NSAIDs often are used as the first line of treatment to manage pain and attenuate
activated inflammatory cascades after muscle injury;18,19 however, a cyclooxygenase-2­–
specific inhibitor (NS-398)20 blocks proliferation and maturation of differentiated
myogenic precursor cells and upregulates TGF-ß1. This process results in fibrotic tissue
development and formation at the injury site. Reduced neutrophil and macrophage
infiltration have been observed in managed muscles, indicating that the delayed skeletal
muscle healing after NS-398 management may be influenced by the anti-inflammatory
effect of NS-398. Therefore, the use of cyclooxygenase-2–specific inhibitors to manage
skeletal muscle injuries warrants caution because of delayed muscle regeneration and
increasing fibrotic deposition.21
Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation Protocol
The acute management of muscle injuries generally includes rest, ice, compression, and
elevation protocol.

Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation Protocol
Immediate application of the rest, ice, compression, and elevation protocol reduces
bleeding at the site of muscle injury. Immobilization prevents retraction of the muscle
edges, reduces additional hematoma formation, and reduces the size of the fibrotic
scar.22 Although immobilization is beneficial immediately postinjury, it causes muscle
fiber atrophy, loss of strength, and excessive connective tissue deposition after more
than a few days of immobility and, therefore, is detrimental to muscle regeneration.23
Optimal return to muscle function can be maximized via relatively early mobilization
(approximately 3 to 5 days postinjury), followed by progressive strengthening, stretching,
and a graduated return to activity.

Blood-Flow Restriction Training
Blood-flow restriction training stimulates muscle strength and hypertrophy gains at much
lower loads than traditional methods, allowing patients to return to sports activity sooner.

Blood-Flow Restriction Training
The American College of Sports Medicine24 established recommendations for strength
training, with intensities greater than 70% of one repetition maximum to stimulate
muscle protein synthesis and satellite-cell activity and decrease proteolysis.25,26 Blood
flow restriction training involves the use of inflatable cuffs to apply external pressure to
restrict venous return while maintaining arterial flow during low-intensity strength
training. Blood-flow restriction training is safe and effective at increasing muscular
strength and endurance in elderly individuals and athletes and in individuals undergoing
rehabilitation programs after injury.27,28
Orthobiologic and Cell Therapies
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a source of blood cells and biologic factors that has unknown
effects on skeletal muscle healing; however, evidence suggests that platelet-poor plasma may
aid in muscle healing.
Combining PRP and losartan blocks fibrosis and enhances skeletal muscle healing.
Cell therapy involves the use of skeletal-muscle–derived stem/progenitor cells, including
muscle-derived stem cells (MDSCs).

and bioactive factors (eg, cytokines, growth factors) above physiologic concentrations,
including platelet-derived growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, and
endothelial growth factor. Injured skeletal muscle treated via PRP may demonstrate
some therapeutic effects in reducing injury-induced pain, while reducing time to return

The major contributor to ECM production and scar-tissue deposition at the site of
muscle injury is TGF-ß1. Therefore, current efforts are focused on finding agents that
decrease TGF-ß1 production and/or block its action to effectively reduce the fibrotic
response. A combinatorial approach of PRP and losartan, a hypertension medication to
antagonize the action of TGF-ß1, is a compelling treatment option to increase
myogenesis while decreasing fibrosis formation in vivo.30
The MDSCs isolated from skeletal muscle are considered a subpopulation of satellite
cells. The essential role of MDSC transplantation in skeletal muscle is induction of
neovascularization. If injected 4 days after muscle injury, MDSC markedly increases
angiogenesis and reduces scar tissue development via higher expression of vascular
endothelial growth factor;31 however, MDSC application is hindered by cell survival, and
no standard cell concentration recommendation has been noted to achieve a desirable
clinical outcome. Therefore, the use of MDSCs is limited.
